title: Cleaning sequence, routine cleaning and checklists
audience: Cleaning and support workers who clean patient rooms, clinics, waiting areas and shared rooms in healthcare settings.
learningOutcomes: Order the tasks in a room from the least contaminated area to the most contaminated area.
Explain why a checklist is used for routine cleaning.
Describe the routine floor and bench cleaning steps for a clinic room.

instruction.heading: Work from clean to dirty and from high to low
instruction.body: The order of work protects surfaces you have already cleaned. Clean from high to low, so that dust and splashes fall onto areas you have not cleaned yet. Clean from the least contaminated surface to the most contaminated one, and finish in the most contaminated area. Wipe benches and tables before vacuuming or mopping, so that anything falling from them is picked up by the floor clean. Starting in the cleanest room and finishing in the dirtiest is the same principle applied to the whole area.

instruction.heading: Routine cleaning and cleaning before and after tasks
instruction.body: Routine cleaning runs at the opening and closing of each day, around specified tasks, and at intervals the schedule fixes. The guide wants benches and tables cleaned around each session and whenever they appear dirty. Wipe the surface with a mild detergent dissolved in warm water, then dry it with a single-use towel. Swap in a clean cloth for every new area so a single soiled cloth cannot spread contamination through the room. Any soiled surface, or any surface a patient touched, is wiped between patients with the same approach.

instruction.heading: Floors and walls
instruction.body: Carpeted areas get daily vacuuming, and hard floors get daily vacuuming followed by mopping. Dampen the floor with detergent solution, then pick up the surplus with a clean, dry cloth or mop. In a poorly ventilated or chilly room, wipe the floor by hand so moisture does not linger. Any wet area must be signed to stop slips and falls. Walls can be cleaned less often than floors, except where they sit in a soiled area or may be splashed. A mild solution in warm water is gentler on wall finishes and on the hands of the worker than hot water; if hot water cannot be avoided, switch to heavier gloves.

instruction.heading: Checklists, posters and hot spots
instruction.body: A checklist shows what has been done and stops a task being missed, so tick each item when it is finished and report any item you could not complete. Cleaning posters placed on the walls help to show the order. Surfaces that many hands touch, for instance handles on doors, wall switches, flush levers, keyboards, bed controls, call bells and wheelchair grips, need cleaning more often than the rest, and the schedule sets how often. The minimum frequencies for these items are set out in “High-touch items: minimum intervals for patient rooms”.

procedure: Read the area schedule and checklist before you start, and note any item that needs a specific product.
Put on gloves and any other protective item the product label requires.
Start with the least contaminated area and work from high to low.
Wipe benches, tables and other surfaces, then clean the floor.
Clean the hot spots at the frequency the schedule states.
Dry the surfaces, sign any wet floor, tick the checklist, and clean and store your equipment.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner in a dental practice must clean the reception area and the treatment room.
workedExamples.reasoning: The reception area is normally the less contaminated space, so it is cleaned first. The treatment room, which has the most contact with body fluid, is cleaned last, in line with the schedule and the zone rules in “Clean zones, contaminated zones and signage”.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner mops a floor and then wipes a bench that has been splashed during the work.
workedExamples.reasoning: The bench should have been wiped first. Wiping after mopping lets debris and splashes land on the clean floor, so the mopping was wasted and the floor has to be done again.

equipmentAndPpe: Disposable gloves and any protective item the label requires
Neutral detergent and warm water, or the facility product for the surface
Disposable paper towel and clean cloths for each area

commonErrors.error: Mopping before the bench and the walls have been wiped.
commonErrors.prevention: Wipe the surfaces first, then clean the floor last.

commonErrors.error: Starting in the most contaminated room.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the clean-to-dirty order on the schedule.

commonErrors.error: Ticking the checklist before a task is finished.
commonErrors.prevention: Tick each item only when it is complete, and report what was missed.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: A wet floor needs a warning notice for as long as it stays wet, so people do not slip.
Use the protective items that the product label and the facility procedure require. Do not mix cleaning products unless the label allows it.
Use the frequency your facility sets.
Completing this lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to perform regulated work.

qualityStandard: Learner orders the tasks in a sample room from least to most contaminated, with reasons.
Learner states the reason for wiping surfaces before mopping.
Learner completes a checklist with every item ticked only when done.
documentationEvidence: Completed checklist with date, area and initials, and a note of any item not completed.
summary: Work downward, and move from the least soiled surface to the most soiled one.
Wipe surfaces before mopping, and sign any wet floor.
Hot spots need more frequent cleaning, and the checklist shows what is done.

knowledgeChecks.question: A room has a bench, a floor and a splashed wall. What is the correct order?
options: Mop the floor first, then wipe the bench and finish with the wall
Wipe the splashed wall after mopping and then wipe the bench again today
Begin with the cleanest surfaces, work downward, and leave the floor for the end
Clean the floor first to keep the bench dry and then wipe the wall last

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should benches be wiped before vacuuming and mopping?
options: Because wiping dries the bench faster and the bench is then polished
So that any debris that falls is collected by the floor clean
Because vacuuming damages the bench and the vacuum hose scratches it
Because mopping must be done last to save water and water is saved

knowledgeChecks.question: A corridor floor is being mopped. What must also be done while it is wet?
options: Nothing, as long as it looks clean
Post a wet-floor sign while it is wet
Ask a visitor to walk over it to dry it
Leave the mop in the middle of the floor
